Justinian I. A sixth-century Byzantine emperor whose ambitions to restore Roman imperial power across the Mediterranean shaped the medieval world for centuries. He commissioned monumental works like the Hagia Sophia, reformed the law through the Justinian Code, and launched military campaigns that temporarily reconquered vast territories in North Africa and the Mediterranean. Though his reign expanded Byzantine power to its greatest territorial extent, plague, warfare, and economic strain ultimately undermined his vision and left the empire exhausted.

Born around 482, Justinian became emperor in 527 and ruled until 565, a reign spanning four decades of constant warfare and ambitious building. He appointed his best general, Belisarius, to reconquer former Roman territories, and through successive campaigns, North Africa, Sicily, and Italy were reclaimed from barbarian kingdoms. Justinian commissioned the Justinian Code, a comprehensive legal compilation that organized Roman law and became the foundation of European law for centuries. His greatest architectural achievement was the Hagia Sophia, built between 532 and 537; it remains the greatest architectural achievement of the Byzantine age and an enduring symbol of Byzantine civilization. His reign coincided with the Plague of Justinian from 541 to 549, which killed millions and undermined his military and economic achievements. By his death, the empire had expanded to include North Africa, the Mediterranean coast, and reconquered Rome itself, but was financially and militarily exhausted from four decades of warfare. The Byzantine Empire he expanded would eventually face the fall of Constantinople, a distant future event whose roots lay in the exhaustion that Justinian's constant campaigns had caused, draining resources that future emperors would desperately need to defend against Ottoman advance.
